enonce_markdown: Consider the proposition: "All traders at Mokolo market are licensed." Which of the following is its contradictory?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On the traditional square of opposition, contradictories always have opposite truth values. The contradictory of an A proposition is the O proposition with the same subject and predicate; the contradictory of an E proposition is the I proposition.

### Solution

The given proposition is an **A** proposition (All $S$ are $P$). Its contradictory is the **O** proposition: "Some traders at Mokolo market are not licensed." If the A proposition is true, this one is false, and if the A proposition is false, this one is true.

The other options are errors commonly made:

- "No traders ... are licensed" is the **E** proposition, the contrary of A: both can be false together.
- "Some traders ... are licensed" is the **I** proposition, the subaltern of A: it follows from A, it does not contradict it.
- "All licensed persons are traders ..." is the simple converse of A, which is not an equivalent proposition.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: No traders at Mokolo market are licensed.
Some traders at Mokolo market are not licensed.
Some traders at Mokolo market are licensed.
All licensed persons are traders at Mokolo market.

enonce_markdown: Suppose that the proposition "Some nurses are not teachers" is true. What can be said about the truth of the proposition "Some nurses are teachers"?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Sub-contraries are the I and O propositions with the same subject and predicate. They cannot both be false, but they can both be true. So the truth of one leaves the other open, while the falsity of one forces the other to be true.

### Solution

"Some nurses are not teachers" is an **O** proposition and "Some nurses are teachers" is its sub-contrary **I**. The truth of O does not settle I: there are situations where some nurses are teachers and some are not (both true), and situations where no nurse is a teacher (I false).

The I proposition is therefore **undetermined (doubtful)**.

The other options misuse the square: sub-contraries do not have to share the same truth value, and O is not the contradictory or the contrary of I (the contradictory of O is A).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: True, because sub-contraries must always have the same truth value.
False, because the two propositions are contradictories.
Undetermined, because sub-contraries can both be true but cannot both be false.
False, because the two propositions are contraries.

enonce_markdown: Which of the following immediate inferences is valid?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Conversion interchanges subject and predicate. It is valid by simple conversion for E and I propositions only. A converts only per accidens (to an I proposition), and O has no valid converse. Check which proposition is being converted before accepting an inference.

### Solution

Option A: "No snakes are mammals; therefore no mammals are snakes." An E proposition converts simply, so this is **valid**.

The other options are invalid:

- "All farmers are cocoa growers; therefore all cocoa growers are farmers" is the simple conversion of an A proposition. If farmers are only some of the cocoa growers, the premise is true and the conclusion false.
- "Some students are not prefects; therefore some prefects are not students" is the conversion of an O proposition, which has no valid converse: all prefects may well be students.
- "Some bikes are not cheap; therefore no bikes are cheap" passes from an O to an E proposition, which are not related by any valid inference (O is the subaltern of E, not the other way round).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: No snakes are mammals; therefore no mammals are snakes.
All farmers are cocoa growers; therefore all cocoa growers are farmers.
Some students are not prefects; therefore some prefects are not students.
Some bikes are not cheap; therefore no bikes are cheap.

enonce_markdown: The proposition "All the members of the choir are students" is false. What can be inferred about the truth values of E ("No members of the choir are students"), I ("Some members of the choir are students") and O ("Some members of the choir are not students") respectively?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use the square of opposition. The falsity of a universal proposition does not settle its contrary or its subaltern, but it fixes its contradictory: contradictories always have opposite truth values.

### Solution

The given proposition is an **A** proposition and it is false.

- **O** is the contradictory of A, so O is **true**.
- **E** is the contrary of A. Contraries cannot both be true, but they can both be false, so the falsity of A leaves E **doubtful** (the choir may contain some students and some non-students, or no student at all).
- **I** is the subaltern of A. The falsity of the universal does not determine the particular: I is **doubtful**.

So E, I and O are respectively doubtful, doubtful and true. The other options keep the pattern which holds when A is *true* (E false, I true, O false) or wrongly treat E or I as settled.

**Answer: D.**

enonce_markdown:
Consider the A proposition: "All members of the Debate Club are students of Form Five."

(a) Give its obverse.
(b) Give its valid converse.
(c) Give its contrapositive.
(d) Explain why "All students of Form Five are members of the Debate Club" is not a valid converse.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Obversion changes the quality of the proposition and replaces the predicate by its complement; it is valid for all four forms. Conversion interchanges subject and predicate; an A proposition converts only per accidens, into an I proposition. Contraposition replaces each term by its complement and interchanges them; for A it keeps the form A.

### Solution

**(a) Obverse.** Change the quality (A becomes E) and complement the predicate: **No members of the Debate Club are persons who are not students of Form Five.**

**(b) Valid converse.** Interchange the terms. For an A proposition the converse is per accidens, an I proposition: **Some students of Form Five are members of the Debate Club.**

**(c) Contrapositive.** Complement both terms and interchange them: **All persons who are not students of Form Five are persons who are not members of the Debate Club.**

**(d)** In the original proposition "students of Form Five" is the predicate of an A proposition, so it is undistributed: the members may be only some of the Form Five students. The simple converse would claim something about *all* Form Five students, which the original does not say. The premise can be true and this "converse" false (if some Form Five students never joined the club).

enonce_markdown:
The proposition "Some taxi drivers in Bamenda are teetotallers" (an I proposition) is false.

(a) State the truth value of the A, E and O propositions with the same subject and predicate, giving the relation of the square of opposition which justifies each answer.
(b) Give the obverse of the E proposition and its truth value.
(c) Give the converse of the original I proposition and its truth value.
(d) A student says: "I is false, so A is true, because A and I are contraries." Show what is wrong with this reasoning.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Start from the given truth value and move along the square: contradictories take opposite values; if a subaltern is false, its superaltern is false; sub-contraries cannot both be false. Obversion and simple conversion of I give propositions equivalent to the original, hence with the same truth value.

### Solution

**(a)** The given proposition I is false.

| Proposition | Truth value | Justification |
|:-|:-:|:-|
| E: No taxi drivers in Bamenda are teetotallers | **True** | E is the contradictory of I, so it has the opposite value |
| A: All taxi drivers in Bamenda are teetotallers | **False** | A is the superaltern of I; if A were true, I would be true. Falsity passes upward from the particular |
| O: Some taxi drivers in Bamenda are not teetotallers | **True** | O is the sub-contrary of I; sub-contraries cannot both be false |

**(b)** The obverse of the E proposition is **All taxi drivers in Bamenda are persons who are not teetotallers**. Obversion yields an equivalent proposition, so it is **true**.

**(c)** The converse of the I proposition is **Some teetotallers are taxi drivers in Bamenda**. I converts simply, so it is equivalent to the original and therefore **false**.

**(d)** The student confuses two relations. A and I are not contraries: I is the *subaltern* of A. The contrary of A is E. From the falsity of I one can only infer, by subalternation, that A is false; the claim "A is true" is also impossible, because A true would force I to be true.
